title: Who Chose 10,000 Steps?

segments.speaker: banker
segments.text: Keep walking. You are only at eight thousand four hundred.

segments.speaker: javelina
segments.text: I've been walking all evening. What happens if I stop?

segments.speaker: banker
segments.text: Sixteen hundred more. Ten thousand steps a day. Everybody knows the rule.

segments.speaker: javelina
segments.text: Everybody? Did a doctor choose that number? A scientist? Who actually checked?

segments.speaker: banker
segments.text: Look at your watch. That little thing knows what you need.

segments.speaker: javelina
segments.text: Then who told the watch? Where did its rule come from?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Tokyo. Nineteen sixty-four. Olympic fever fills the streets. A clock company has a little box to sell. In nineteen sixty-five, Yamasa calls it the ten-thousand-step meter. A neat number. A memorable symbol. An easy slogan. But the origin is messier. Yamasa credits an earlier walking campaign involving doctors and journalists. A campaign goal still isn't a biological boundary. Advertisements repeat it. Walking clubs. Magazines. Fitness trackers. Soon, the same target glows on wrists everywhere. Repeated long enough, a convenient target starts to sound compulsory. In twenty nineteen, researchers studying older women found benefits below ten thousand. That wasn't evidence for everybody. A twenty twenty-five review covered fifty-seven adult studies. Meaningful health benefits appeared at lower counts. Seven thousand was a practical marker, not a magic finish line. These were adult studies, not a universal rule for every age and ability. Back in town, Javelina thinks missing the target makes his whole walk worthless. He lowers the watch. Straightens his back. Stands up. Keeps walking. The Banker waits for a sale that isn't coming. Walking was useful. The universal rule was the story. Which other rules have you never questioned?
